analogy.p: Hang the same 1 N weight on a stiff garage-door spring and on a soft slinky. The slinky stretches several centimetres while the garage-door spring barely moves: the slinky has a small spring constant, the garage-door spring a large one. Double the weight and each stretches twice as far, as Hooke's law says, until you pull a slinky so far that the coils bend open and it never goes back to its old shape, which is passing the limit of proportionality. The analogy breaks down because a real spring's restoring force comes from the twisting of the metal wire and the forces between its atoms, and a slinky is far less ideal than a lab spring, so its straight-line range is much shorter.
analogy.t: A stiff garage-door spring versus a soft slinky

bullets: To stretch a spring you need two forces acting in opposite directions on the two ends: one pulling each way (tension).
To compress a spring you need two forces pushing inwards on the two ends.
To bend a beam, such as a ruler held at one end, you need forces that act at different points in different directions (for example the clamp pushing up and your finger pushing down).
If only one unbalanced force acts the object accelerates instead; shape change needs the forces to be applied to different parts of the object.
Deformation is a **contact force** effect: the forces are applied where the object touches whatever is pulling or pushing it.
Link to Newton's third law: when you pull the spring, the spring pulls back on you with an equal and opposite force.
Link to energy: doing work to deform an object transfers energy to the **elastic potential energy store** of that object.
core.h: Why you need more than one force to deform an object
core.p: A single force acting on an object usually just changes its motion (it accelerates the object) or turns it. To **change the shape** of an object, that is to **stretch, compress or bend** it, there must be **more than one force** acting on it, and the forces must act in a way that squeezes or pulls different parts of the object in different directions. If you pull on a spring that is attached to a fixed clamp, the clamp supplies the second force, equal and opposite to your pull, which is why the spring stretches instead of simply speeding away.

bullets: **Elastic deformation**: the object goes back to its original shape and size when the load is removed, and the energy stored is released.

**Inelastic deformation**: the object is permanently changed (it has a **permanent extension**) because the force has been too large; the atoms/layers have moved past the point where they can spring back.

A spring that is stretched too far will not return to its original length: it has passed its **elastic limit**. Strictly the elastic limit is the point beyond which permanent deformation occurs; for most springs at GCSE it is close to the limit of proportionality.
Everyday elastic objects: springs, trampolines, rubber bands used gently, bungee ropes, bows, trampoline surfaces, diving boards.
Everyday inelastic behaviour: a paper clip bent open, plasticine squashed, a spring stretched too far, a car crumple zone (designed to deform permanently to absorb energy).
The key question for a diagram: if unloading retraces the loading line on a force-extension graph it is elastic; if it ends at a non-zero extension when the force is zero, it is inelastic.
Why it matters: engineers must keep forces below the elastic limit for springs, suspension and cables so that they keep working.
core.p: When an object is deformed there are two possible outcomes. If the object returns to its **original shape and length** when the deforming forces are removed, the deformation was **elastic**. An object that has been elastically deformed is called an **elastically deformed object**, and it stores energy in its **elastic potential energy store** while it is deformed. If the object does **not** return to its original shape when the forces are removed, it has been **inelastically deformed**, and it is left permanently stretched, bent or squashed.

bullets: Equation in words: **force (N) = spring constant (N/m) x extension (m)**; symbols **F = k e**.
The equation also applies to **compression**; in that case e is the compression (the amount the spring is squashed by), the change in length from its natural length.
Rearrangements: **e = F / k** (to find extension) and **k = F / e** (to find the spring constant).
Units: F in newtons (N), e in metres (m), k in newtons per metre (N/m). **Convert cm or mm to m before you calculate**: 12 cm = 0.12 m, 45 mm = 0.045 m.

'Directly proportional' means the line goes through the origin; a straight line that does not go through the origin is linear but not proportional (this can appear if extension is measured badly or the spring was already stretched by its own weight).
Hooke's law only works up to the **limit of proportionality**. Beyond it, F = k e no longer gives the right extension.
The force F here is the force **applied to the spring**. In a hanging-mass experiment this is the **weight** of the masses, W = m g (with g = 9.8 N/kg).
A stiff spring (large k) needs a large force for each metre of extension; a soft spring (small k) stretches a lot for a small force.
core.h: Hooke's law: force is proportional to extension
core.p: For an elastically deformed spring that has **not** been stretched past its limit of proportionality, the **extension is directly proportional to the force applied**. This is the relationship usually called **Hooke's law**, and the equation is **force exerted on a spring = spring constant x extension**, or in symbols **F = k e**. Because the relationship is proportional, doubling the force doubles the extension, and a graph of force against extension is a **straight line through the origin**.

bullets: Definition to learn: the spring constant is the force per unit extension, k = F / e, for a spring within its limit of proportionality.
On a **force-extension graph (force on the y-axis)**, the **gradient of the straight section equals the spring constant k**, because gradient = change in F / change in e = k.
If the graph is drawn the other way round (extension on y-axis, force on x-axis), the gradient equals **1 / k**, not k. Always check which axis is which.
A steeper force-extension line means a larger k, so a stiffer spring.
Typical values: a spring from a school kit might have k of 10 to 100 N/m; a car suspension spring has k of order 10 000 N/m or more.
Two different springs can be compared by plotting their lines on the same axes: the steeper one is stiffer.
The spring constant is a **property of the spring, not of the load**: using heavier masses does not change k (until you go past the limit of proportionality).
Common unit trap: if you get k in N/cm from a graph, convert to N/m by multiplying by 100.
core.p: The **spring constant** tells you how stiff a spring is. It is the **force needed to produce 1 metre of extension** (or compression), and it is measured in **newtons per metre (N/m)**. A spring with a spring constant of 50 N/m needs 50 N to stretch it by 1 m (or 5 N to stretch it by 0.10 m) as long as it stays within its limit of proportionality. The value of k depends on the spring itself: its material, thickness of the wire, number of coils and coil diameter.

bullets: **e = new length - natural length**. Example: natural length 8.0 cm, stretched length 11.5 cm, so e = 3.5 cm = 0.035 m.
If a question gives a total length, always subtract the natural length first.
A spring that has no load on it has e = 0 and F = 0, so the graph starts at the origin.
In the required practical, measure the natural length with **no masses (or only the hanger, if you decide to treat it as the starting load and say so)** and then subtract it from every later reading.
Work to the same number of decimal places as the ruler allows: a ruler marked in mm gives readings to the nearest 1 mm (0.001 m), with a resolution of 1 mm.
Compression follows the same rule F = k e with e as the amount of squashing; for a spring in a car or a mattress the same equation applies.
Link to maths: this is a subtraction of two measurements, so the **uncertainty** in e is larger than in a single reading; careful, accurate readings matter.
core.p: The **natural length** (original length) of a spring is its length with no forces applied. The **extension** is how much longer the spring is than its natural length, so **extension e = stretched length - natural length**. For a compressed spring the **compression** is natural length minus compressed length. The extension is the quantity in F = k e, **not** the total length, and this is one of the most common causes of lost marks.

bullets: **Linear**: straight line graph; extension changes by equal amounts for equal increases in force; F = k e applies.
**Non-linear**: curved line; the gradient changes; F = k e does **not** apply.
The **limit of proportionality** is the point on the graph where the straight line stops and the curve begins.

On the straight part, the spring is deformed elastically and obeys Hooke's law; beyond the limit the spring may still be elastic for a little way, but then reaches the elastic limit and starts to deform permanently.

For many springs the limit of proportionality and the elastic limit are close together, so exam questions often treat 'goes beyond the limit of proportionality' as the spring being permanently damaged; read the question wording.
Rubber bands and some materials are non-linear from the start: their force-extension graph is curved even at small extensions.

Describe the difference in an exam: 'the first section is a straight line (linear), so force is directly proportional to extension; after the limit of proportionality the line curves, so force is not proportional to extension.'
To find the spring constant from a graph with a curved section, use only the **straight section**.
core.h: Linear and non-linear relationships and the limit of proportionality
core.p: A **linear relationship** between force and extension is one where the graph is a **straight line**; if the line passes through the origin the quantities are **directly proportional**. For a spring, the graph is a straight line **up to the limit of proportionality**. Beyond that point the graph **curves**: the relationship is **non-linear**, and equal increases in force no longer produce equal increases in extension. For a typical spring the extension then increases **faster** than predicted, so the graph bends towards the extension axis.

bullets: Plotting: choose scales that are easy to read (1, 2, 5 or 10 per square) and use at least half the grid.
Line of best fit: roughly equal numbers of points above and below the line; the line should go through the origin if the relationship is proportional.
**Gradient** method: draw a large triangle on the straight section, read the changes ΔF and Δe, and calculate k = ΔF / Δe with units N/m. A large triangle reduces percentage error.
If extensions are plotted in cm, convert to m before calculating the gradient, or convert the final answer.
**Anomalous** points are those that do not fit the pattern; they are circled and ignored when drawing the line (and the reading should be repeated if possible).
Reading values from the graph: to find the extension for a given force, go across from the force to the line then down to the extension axis (and use dotted construction lines).
The limit of proportionality is where the data begins to depart from the straight line, so state the force and extension at that point if asked.
Compare two springs: the one with the steeper gradient has the greater spring constant.
core.h: Force-extension graphs: drawing and reading them
core.p: Always plot **force on the y-axis** and **extension on the x-axis** for a spring (this is the convention that makes the gradient equal to k). Use sensible scales so that the points fill more than half of the graph paper in each direction, label both axes with quantity **and unit**, plot points with small neat crosses, and draw a **line of best fit**: a straight ruler line through the linear points (not necessarily through every point, and ignoring anomalies), and a smooth curve for the non-linear section.

bullets: Equation in words: **elastic potential energy (J) = 0.5 x spring constant (N/m) x (extension (m))²**; Ee = ½ k e².
The **energy stored equals the work done** in stretching the spring if no energy is dissipated, because energy is conserved.
On a force-extension graph the **area under the line equals the work done** (energy stored). For a straight line through the origin the area is a triangle with area ½ x base x height = ½ e F.
Because e is **squared**, doubling the extension makes the stored energy **four times** bigger; tripling the extension makes it nine times bigger.

When a stretched spring is released, the elastic store is **transferred to the kinetic energy store** (the spring moves) and some is dissipated as heat and sound to the thermal store of the surroundings.
Typical energy transfer chains: a catapult or toy dart gun (elastic to kinetic), a trampoline (elastic to kinetic to gravitational potential), a pogo stick.
Higher-challenge: if a spring launches a mass upwards, equate ½ k e² to m g h (ideal case, no losses) to find the height.
Do not confuse **F = k e** (a force) with **Ee = ½ k e²** (an energy). Check the units: if the answer should be joules you must have the ½ and the squared extension.
core.h: Work done in stretching a spring and elastic potential energy
core.p: Stretching or compressing a spring means a force acts over a distance, so **work is done** on the spring. This energy is transferred to the **elastic potential energy store** of the spring (the energy stored in an elastically deformed object). Because the force grows steadily from zero to its final value F as the extension grows from zero to e, the **average force is half of the final force**, so the work done is W = average force x distance = ½ F e. Substituting F = k e gives **elastic potential energy: Ee = ½ k e²**, where Ee is in joules (J), k in N/m and e in m. This equation works **only up to the limit of proportionality**.

bullets: **Set-up**: clamp the spring from a stand at the top; hang a mass hanger from the bottom; place a **metre ruler vertically** next to the spring, held in a second clamp or standing on the bench, with a **pointer or marker** (a small piece of tape or a pin) on the bottom of the spring to help read the scale. Check the ruler is vertical (use a set square).
**Method step 1**: measure the **natural length** of the spring with the hanger only (or no load) and record it.

**Step 2**: add a 100 g slotted mass (weight about 0.98 N, using g = 9.8 N/kg); wait until the spring is **still**; read the new length from the ruler with your **eye level with the pointer** to avoid parallax error.
**Step 3**: calculate **extension = new length - natural length** and **force = mass x 9.8**.
**Step 4**: add masses one at a time (at least 5 to 8 readings) up to a safe maximum, recording length each time. Do **not** exceed the limit of proportionality unless investigating it deliberately.
**Step 5**: remove the masses one at a time and read the length again (optional), to test whether the spring returns to the original length (elastic).
**Step 6**: **repeat** the experiment and calculate a mean extension for each force to improve reliability.
**Step 7**: plot a graph of force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis); draw a best-fit line; find the gradient to get k.
core.h: Required practical: investigating the relationship between force and extension for a spring
core.p: The aim is to **investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring**. The independent variable is the **force applied to the spring** (changed by adding masses, with weight W = m g), and the dependent variable is the **extension** of the spring. The method relies on measuring the length of the spring accurately each time a new mass is added, then calculating extension by subtracting the natural length.

bullets: **Risk and control**: masses can fall onto feet, so wear **safety goggles**, keep feet clear of the stand, use a **mat or box of sand/foam** beneath the masses, and clamp the stand firmly (or add a G-clamp to the bench). Springs can snap back and hit the eyes if over-stretched.
**Parallax error**: read the ruler at eye level with the pointer, not from above or below.
**Zero error / starting point**: record the natural length first, and measure extension, not length.
**Oscillation**: wait for the spring to stop bouncing before reading, or the reading will be wrong.
**Resolution**: a ruler graduated in mm has a resolution of 1 mm; use a mm scale for small extensions, and larger masses for larger extensions to reduce the percentage uncertainty.
**Reliability**: repeat readings and calculate a **mean**; if repeat results differ a lot, the data is not repeatable.
**Systematic error**: if the masses are slightly different from labelled (e.g. rusty), or the ruler is not vertical, all values shift in the same direction; check masses and ruler.
**Random error**: caused by misreadings or bouncing; reduced by repeating and averaging.
**Validity**: the investigation is valid if only the force is changed while other variables are controlled and the right quantity (extension) is measured.
core.h: Required practical: control variables, accuracy, safety and sources of error
core.p: A good answer needs the **variables** named correctly, a clear explanation of how to improve accuracy and reliability, and sensible safety. The **independent variable** is the force (hung masses), the **dependent variable** is the extension, and the **control variables** include using the **same spring**, the same ruler, measuring from the same point on the spring each time, and keeping the temperature steady. Without control variables the results are not a fair test.

bullets: Conclusion template: 'The graph is a straight line through the origin, so extension is directly proportional to force. The gradient is k = ___ N/m.'
If the graph curves at higher forces: 'beyond ___ N the line curves, so the spring has passed its limit of proportionality and no longer obeys Hooke's law.'
Check for **permanent extension**: if after removing all masses the spring is longer than at the start, it has been stretched past its elastic limit (inelastic deformation).
Hysteresis (not required by the spec, but useful): loading and unloading curves may not match for rubber, because the material does not return the same way.

Evaluate: more readings between zero and the limit give a better line; use smaller mass steps near the limit to find it precisely; use a travelling microscope or a set square pointer to improve measurement.
The percentage uncertainty in a small extension is large, since the uncertainty in each length reading (about 1 mm) is a big fraction of the extension; so use larger extensions within the limit.
Anomalies: identify by looking for points off the best-fit line; repeat those readings; do not include them in the mean.
Use the gradient triangle and show working, including the unit conversion from cm to m.
Link: the same investigation approach (vary one input, measure one output, control the rest) applies to many other required practicals.
core.h: Analysing results, drawing conclusions and evaluating
core.p: After plotting force against extension, look for the straight section. If it is a straight line through the origin, the conclusion is: **'force is directly proportional to extension, so the spring obeys Hooke's law, up to the limit of proportionality'**. Calculate the spring constant from the gradient of the straight section. You can then use k to predict the extension for new forces, and the area under the graph to find the elastic energy stored.

bullets: Hanging mass: at equilibrium **spring force = weight**, so k e = m g, therefore e = m g / k (g = 9.8 N/kg).
Compressed spring launching a trolley: Ee (spring) = Ek (trolley) if no losses, so ½ k e² = ½ m v² and v = e x square root of (k / m).

Dropping a mass onto a spring: gravitational potential energy converts to elastic potential energy (m g (h + e) = ½ k e², where h is the drop before touching the spring and e the compression) at maximum compression, if you ignore losses.
Equation for the force: use F = k e where F is the **resultant force acting on the spring** (the force pulling one end relative to the other).
Unit checks: k in N/m x e in m = N; ½ x N/m x m² = N m = J.
Use the correct value of g in the question (9.8 N/kg in AQA data; some papers use 10 N/kg: use what is given).
Do the energy conversion carefully: only use ½ k e² for the energy **stored in the spring**, not for any other store.
core.h: Combining Hooke's law with other equations
core.p: Exam questions often combine F = k e with other equations. The most common are **weight W = m g**, **work done W = F s** and **Ee = ½ k e²**, and the energy conversions between energy stores. If a mass hangs at rest from a vertical spring, the spring force upwards equals the weight downwards (balanced forces), so k e = m g and e = m g / k.

bullets: Why does the graph curve? Beyond the limit, the forces between the atoms/coils no longer produce a restoring force proportional to the extension, and the material begins to deform permanently.
Compare springs: spring A with a graph gradient of 60 N/m is twice as stiff as spring B with 30 N/m; for the same force A extends half as much.
Is the force within the proportional range? Check whether F is below the force at the limit of proportionality shown on the graph.
Energy: area under a non-linear curve (after the limit) is not ½ k e²; estimate by counting squares.
Bungee jumps: the cord stores elastic energy as the jumper falls, converting gravitational potential energy; the cord must stay within its elastic range.
Safety: crumple zones deform inelastically on purpose to absorb kinetic energy; this is useful inelastic deformation.
Link to Newton's laws: at equilibrium the spring force balances the weight (Newton's first law); on release the unbalanced spring force accelerates the mass (Newton's second law).
Link to work and power: stretching a spring is an example of work done by a force, W = F s, but with a changing force, hence the average force.
core.h: Higher tier and exam links: reasoning, comparison and links to other topics
core.p: At the top grades you are expected to reason with these ideas, not just plug numbers into equations. That includes explaining why a spring's graph curves, comparing two springs, deciding whether a given force is within the proportional range, and linking the elastic store to energy transfers and to design (shock absorbers, trampolines, bungee jumps, car crumple zones). Remember that Hooke's law is an **approximation** that works over a limited range.

exam: **State/Give/Name (1 mark)**: a single fact, e.g. 'k = F / e' or 'elastic potential energy'. Short, exact wording scores.

**Calculate (2 to 3 marks)**: write the equation (1), substitute with correct units (1), answer with unit (1). Convert cm to m. Show your working: a wrong answer with correct working can still pick up method marks.

**Describe the relationship (2 marks)**: 'extension is directly proportional to force (1) up to the limit of proportionality (1)'. Mention the straight line through the origin if asked about the graph.

**Explain (3 to 4 marks)**: use 'because' and link cause to effect, e.g. 'the line curves because the spring has passed its limit of proportionality (1), so the extension is no longer proportional to force (1)'.

**Describe the required practical (4 to 6 marks)**: include the equipment (clamp, spring, ruler, masses), measure natural length, add masses, measure length, calculate extension, repeat, plot a graph; add the control of variables, repeats and safety for the top band.
**Graph questions**: plot with force on y, extension on x, label axes with units, best-fit line, and use a large triangle to find the gradient; state units N/m.
**Energy questions**: use Ee = ½ k e²; remember to square e. Check that your answer is in joules and is sensible (usually below a few joules for lab springs).
**Spot the limit**: say 'at the point where the graph stops being straight' and quote the force and extension values from the graph.

**Evaluate/improve (2 to 3 marks)**: suggest a specific improvement (read at eye level to remove parallax, use smaller mass increments, repeat and take a mean) and explain what it improves (accuracy or reliability).
**Compare springs**: use the gradient (stiffer = steeper line = bigger k) and quote numbers.
**Command words**: 'Calculate' needs working and units; 'Determine' means find from data or a graph; 'Explain' needs reasons; 'Suggest' means apply knowledge to a new context.

mistakes.r: Extension = stretched length - natural length. Subtract the natural length first.
mistakes.w: Using the total length of the spring as the extension in F = k e.

mistakes.r: Convert extension to metres (divide cm by 100, mm by 1000) before using F = k e or Ee = ½ k e².
mistakes.w: Leaving the extension in cm or mm and getting k = 2000 N/m instead of 20 N/m.

mistakes.r: Elastic potential energy Ee = ½ x k x e²; the extension is squared and there is a half.
mistakes.w: Writing Ee = ½ k e (forgetting to square) or Ee = k e².

mistakes.r: Force is directly proportional to extension (change in length), up to the limit of proportionality.
Directly proportional needs a straight line through the origin; a straight line not through the origin is linear only.
mistakes.w: Saying a straight line graph always means directly proportional.

mistakes.r: Use only the straight (linear) section of the graph below the limit of proportionality.
mistakes.w: Calculating the spring constant using the gradient of the curved section.

mistakes.r: Wait until the spring is still, read at eye level, repeat and calculate a mean to improve reliability.
mistakes.w: Not repeating readings or not waiting for the spring to stop bouncing.

mistakes.r: The limit of proportionality is where the graph stops being a straight line; beyond the elastic limit the deformation is permanent (inelastic), not necessarily broken.
mistakes.w: Saying the limit of proportionality and elastic limit are 'where the spring breaks'.

mistakes.r: The gradient of the force-extension graph is k; the area under it is the work done / energy stored.
mistakes.w: Reading the area under the graph as k.

summary: The specification asks you to explain that deforming an object needs more than one force, to distinguish elastic from inelastic deformation, to use F = k e (Hooke's law) and Ee = ½ k e² for springs within the limit of proportionality, to interpret linear and non-linear force-extension graphs, and to carry out and evaluate the required practical on force and extension. It matters because springs are used in energy stores, suspension and measuring devices, and this is a regular source of calculation and practical marks.

terms.d: A change in shape of an object that is reversed when the deforming force is removed; the object returns to its original shape.
A change in shape that is not reversed when the force is removed; the object is permanently deformed.
An object that has been stretched, compressed or bent but will go back to its original shape when the forces are removed; it stores energy in its elastic potential energy store.
The increase in length of a spring from its natural length: e = stretched length - natural length.
The decrease in length of a spring from its natural length when it is squashed.
The length of a spring when no force is acting on it.
For a spring within its limit of proportionality, the extension is directly proportional to the force applied: F = k e.
The force needed to produce unit extension of a spring (1 m), measured in newtons per metre (N/m); the gradient of the straight section of a force-extension graph.
The point beyond which the force-extension graph stops being a straight line; extension is no longer directly proportional to force.
The maximum force/extension beyond which an object does not return to its original shape; beyond it deformation is permanent.
A relationship that gives a straight-line graph; if it passes through the origin, the two quantities are directly proportional.
A relationship whose graph is a curve; equal changes in one quantity do not give equal changes in the other.
The energy stored in an elastically deformed object, Ee = ½ k e² (up to the limit of proportionality).
Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance, W = F s; equal to the area under a force-extension graph.
Two quantities whose ratio is constant; doubling one doubles the other and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
A force that acts only when two objects are touching, such as the force of a hand stretching a spring.
The smallest change in a quantity that the measuring instrument can detect, e.g. 1 mm on a ruler.
An error caused by reading a scale from an angle rather than with the eye level with the pointer.
A variable that is kept the same in an investigation so that it does not affect the result.

worked.ans: k = 50 N/m; Ee = 0.36 J. Check: ½ F e = 0.5 x 6.0 x 0.12 = 0.36 J, which agrees.
worked.q: A spring has a natural length of 0.20 m. A force of 6.0 N stretches it to a length of 0.32 m. The limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. (a) Calculate the spring constant. (b) Calculate the elastic potential energy stored. [5 marks]
steps: Rearrange F = k e to k = F / e (1 mark).
Ee = ½ k e² = 0.5 x 50 x 0.12² (1 mark).

worked.ans: Extension = 0.1225 m (about 0.12 m); energy stored = 0.30 J.
worked.q: A 0.50 kg mass hangs at rest from a spring with spring constant 40 N/m. Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate (a) the extension of the spring and (b) the energy stored in the spring. [5 marks]
steps: Weight W = m g = 0.50 x 9.8 = 4.9 N (1 mark). At rest, spring force = weight so F = 4.9 N.
e = F / k = 4.9 / 40 = 0.1225 m (1 mark), which is 12 cm to 2 s.f. (0.12 m).
Ee = ½ k e² = 0.5 x 40 x 0.1225² (1 mark).
Check: ½ F e = 0.5 x 4.9 x 0.1225 = 0.300 J (1 mark for consistent unit and answer).

worked.ans: k = 40 N/m; work done = 0.80 J; beyond 8.0 N the graph is non-linear, so Hooke's law no longer applies.
worked.q: A student investigates a spring and plots force against extension. The graph is a straight line from (0, 0) to (0.20 m, 8.0 N), then curves. (a) Calculate the spring constant. (b) Calculate the work done stretching the spring up to 8.0 N. (c) Explain what the curve shows. [6 marks]
steps: k = gradient of the straight section = 8.0 / 0.20 = 40 N/m (2 marks: method and answer).
Work done = area under the graph = ½ x base x height = 0.5 x 0.20 x 8.0 = 0.80 J (2 marks). Check: ½ k e² = 0.5 x 40 x 0.04 = 0.80 J.

The curve shows that after 8.0 N the spring has gone past its limit of proportionality (1 mark), so force is no longer directly proportional to extension and the spring may be permanently deformed (1 mark).
